title: Korach: sounds fair (Numbers 16:3)
hook: Korach says all the congregation is holy; the words are true, the motive is not

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzitzit, fringes to look at, remember and do. Your line was see and remember. Hold on to those fringes; they come back today, in an argument.

A speech can be built entirely out of true sentences. Everyone deserves a voice. The people in charge have been there too long. Why should a few decide for everyone? A listener can agree with every word and still sense something off, once they notice who's speaking, and what that person would get if they won. This week's portion opens with exactly that kind of speech, delivered to Moses' face, in front of a crowd, by his own cousin. And the line at the center of it is hard to argue with.
screen: `A SPEECH MADE OF TRUE SENTENCES.` → `WHO'S SPEAKING?` → `MOSES' OWN COUSIN.`

segments.voice: Korach is a Levite, a grandson of Kohath, from the same family as Moses and Aaron. He gathers Dathan and Abiram, and two hundred fifty respected leaders, and they confront Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?" Every phrase has a source. At Sinai, God called the whole people a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. In Leviticus, holiness was spoken to the whole congregation. Korach echoes the Torah back at Moses. So what's wrong? The rabbis looked under the speech. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says Korach was jealous: a younger cousin had been appointed leader of their clan instead of him. A midrash pictures his opening move. He dresses his followers in cloaks made entirely of blue wool and asks Moses: does a cloak that's all blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? Moses says yes. Korach's crowd laughs. He's using yesterday's commandment to make both the law and Moses look ridiculous. Then Moses answers, and exposes the motive. You Levites, he says, isn't it enough that you serve at the sanctuary? Now you want the priesthood too? He even hands Korach's words back: you take too much upon you. In the rabbis' reading, the claim was that everyone is equal. The goal was to be above.
screen: `ALL THE CONGREGATION ARE HOLY.` · `TRUE WORDS, FROM THE TORAH.` · `A CLOAK ALL OF BLUE.` · `NOW YOU WANT THE PRIESTHOOD TOO?` · then, large: `WHAT'S UNDER THE ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now, at work, at home, online, and say your position to yourself in its best words. Then ask quietly what you'd get if you won: respect, being right, a seat you've wanted, an old score settled? Don't judge what you find; just notice whether the words and the want point the same way.
Korach. The Levite who said all the congregation is holy, true words, carried by a wish to be above them.
Your line: what's under the argument. True words can still carry a want. That's day four hundred fifty-one.

screen: `DAY 451 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KORACH: NOT FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE (AVOT 5:17).`

howItsDone: When the portion Korach is read, Jewish teachers often pair Korach's speech with the midrash of the all-blue cloak, and use it to talk about the difference between a true claim and the reason someone is making it.

chat.says: Korach said the whole congregation is holy. Isn't that true? Why was he wrong?
options: His words echo the Torah, but the rabbis say he used them to reach for power.
Because the Torah says only the priests are holy, not the whole people.
Only because he said it on the Sabbath, when arguing with a leader is forbidden.
chat.meaning: Korach's claim echoed Sinai and Leviticus, but Rashi and the midrash read jealousy under it: the claim was equality, the goal was to be above.

Korach.meaning: the Levite who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron

Dathan.meaning: one of Korach's allies in the rebellion

Sinai.meaning: the mountain where the Torah was given

notes: Numbers 16:3 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; confirm.
Korach's lineage: son of Izhar son of Kohath (Exodus 6:18–21), so a first cousin of Moses and Aaron; the script says 'a grandson of Kohath, from the same family'. Confirm.
The all-blue cloak midrash (Tanchuma Korach 2; Numbers Rabbah 18:3; cited by Rashi on 16:1); confirm citations.
Moses' 'you take too much upon you, ye sons of Levi' is Numbers 16:7; 'seek ye the priesthood also' is 16:10. Paraphrased.

Review pass: 'a younger cousin' means Elizaphan son of Uzziel, Kohath's youngest son (Korach's father Izhar was the second). The jealousy motive and the 'true words, wrong motive' framing in the hook are the rabbinic reading (Rashi, Tanchuma), not the plain text alone; the teach attributes them to the rabbis. Confirm.
